DOCUMENT:
Evaluation Report: Text-Message Reminders in the School Flu Vaccination Programme, 2025-26
Eastvale Public Health Team, February 2026

1. Summary
This report evaluates the use of text-message reminders to parents during the 2025-26 school-aged flu vaccination programme in Eastvale. Uptake was 13 percentage points higher in schools using reminders than in schools that did not. We recommend that reminders be extended to every primary school in the area for 2026-27, with the aim of raising uptake to at least 70% across Eastvale.

2. Background
Children in Reception to Year 6 are offered a nasal flu vaccine in school each autumn. Parents must return a consent form, on paper or through the online consent portal, before the immunisation team visits. Low consent return is the main reason children go unvaccinated: in most schools nearly all children with consent are vaccinated on the day.

In 2025-26, schools could opt in to an automated reminder service. Parents who had not returned consent received up to three text messages in the two weeks before the session, each with a link to the online portal. 38 of Eastvale's 92 primary schools opted in. Opting-in schools were disproportionately those with a full-time school nurse (29 of the 38, compared with 11 of the other 54) and those in the more affluent western half of the area.

3. Results
Table 1. Uptake by reminder status, 2025-26
Group | Schools | Eligible pupils | Consents returned | Vaccinated | Uptake
Reminder schools | 38 | 9,120 | 6,840 | 6,384 | 70.0%
Non-reminder schools | 54 | 12,960 | 7,970 | 7,388 | 57.0%
All schools | 92 | 22,080 | 14,810 | 13,772 | 66.0%

Consent return was 75% in reminder schools and 61% in non-reminder schools. In both groups more than 92% of children with consent were vaccinated, confirming that consent, not attendance on the day, is the binding constraint.

Overall uptake across Eastvale was 66.0%, above the national ambition of 65% for this age group for the first time.

The 13-point difference between reminder and non-reminder schools is the clearest evidence we have on what drives uptake locally. It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points, more than any other intervention we have tried, at a cost of less than ten pence per message.

4. Who is not being reached
Uptake in non-reminder schools varied widely, from 38% to 79%. The lowest-uptake schools are concentrated in the eastern wards, which have higher proportions of families who speak a language other than English at home and higher rates of household mobility. In the 54 non-reminder schools, the school information system holds a valid mobile number for 61% of families, compared with 93% in the reminder schools. Paper consent forms in these schools are also more often returned incomplete, typically with the medical history section blank.

Immunisation team staff report that a second visit (a "mop-up" session) adds between three and six points of uptake where it is offered, but mop-up sessions were held in only 14 schools this year because of staffing.

5. Cost
Each reminder costs £0.08 to send. If all three reminders were sent to every family without consent in the 54 non-reminder schools (about 4,990 families on 2025-26 figures), the cost would be under £1,200 a year. Continuing reminders in the existing 38 schools costs about £550 a year. There is a one-off set-up charge of £2,500 for linking school data to the messaging platform.

6. Recommendation
Because reminders raised uptake by 13 points, extending them to the 54 non-reminder schools should raise uptake there from 57% to around 70%, bringing every part of Eastvale up to the level now seen in the west. This is by far the cheapest route to closing the gap. We recommend that the Health and Wellbeing Board fund reminders for all 92 schools from September 2026, at a total first-year cost of under £5,000, and that the team report on uptake by school at the end of the 2026-27 season.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [arithmetic] at: "Overall uptake across Eastvale was 66.0%, above the national ambition of 65% for this age group for the first time." -- 13,772 vaccinated / 22,080 eligible = 62.4%, not 66.0% (the table's 'All schools' uptake is also wrong). Correctly computed, Eastvale is below, not above, the 65% ambition.
2. [unsupported_causal] at: "It shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points, more than any other intervention we have tried" -- Schools self-selected into reminders, and the document states opting-in schools were disproportionately those with a full-time school nurse (29/38 vs 11/54) and more affluent. The 13-point gap is confounded and cannot be attributed to the reminders.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "extending them to the 54 non-reminder schools should raise uptake there from 57% to around 70%" -- The projection assumes reminders will reach families in the non-reminder schools as they did elsewhere, but the document reports a valid mobile number for only 61% of those families (vs 93% in reminder schools). The recommendation never addresses that roughly 39% of families could not receive a text.

REVIEW:
# Review: Text-Message Reminders in the 2025-26 School Flu Programme

The report is clearly written and the arithmetic mostly holds, but it has one factual error in the headline figures, and its central causal claim and recommendation rest on a comparison that can't support them.

## 1. Calculation error: overall uptake is not 66.0%

Table 1's own numbers give a different total:

- 13,772 vaccinated ÷ 22,080 eligible = **62.4%**, not 66.0%.
- A weighted check agrees: (0.70 × 9,120 + 0.57 × 12,960) ÷ 22,080 ≈ 62.4%.
- Consents returned ÷ eligible is 67.1%, so 66.0% isn't a mislabelled consent rate either.

The consequence is that the statement "above the national ambition of 65% for the first time" is wrong. On these figures Eastvale is about 2.6 points **below** the ambition. This needs correcting in Section 3, and the context for the 70% target in Section 1 should be re-checked. The other table totals (eligible, consents, vaccinated) do sum correctly.

Minor: non-reminder consent return is 61.5% (7,970 ÷ 12,960), reported as 61%.

## 2. The causal claim is not supported

Section 3 says the comparison "shows that text reminders raise uptake by around 13 percentage points". Schools opted in, so this is a self-selected comparison, and the report itself shows the groups differ in ways that plausibly drive uptake:

- **School nurse:** 29 of 38 reminder schools (76%) had a full-time nurse, against 11 of 54 (20%) of the others.
- **Affluence and geography:** reminder schools skew towards the affluent west. Non-reminder schools include the eastern wards with language barriers and high mobility.
- **Data quality:** valid mobile numbers are held for 93% of families in reminder schools but only 61% in the others. Schools with good data systems may differ in many other ways.
- **Motivation:** schools that choose to opt in are likely to be more engaged anyway.

The 13 points is therefore an upper bound on the reminder effect and may include a large share of confounding. The claim that reminders beat "any other intervention we have tried" is also unsupported, since no comparison data are presented. The only other figure given, 3–6 points from mop-up sessions, isn't compared on a like-for-like basis.

**What would strengthen it:**
- Compare each school's 2025-26 uptake with its own 2024-25 baseline (difference-in-differences).
- Stratify by nurse presence and area deprivation, or at least show uptake within those subgroups.
- Report school-level spread and confidence intervals. With only 38 and 54 schools, uncertainty matters.

## 3. The recommendation extrapolates beyond the evidence

"Extending reminders to the 54 schools should raise uptake from 57% to around 70%" assumes the effect transfers unchanged. Section 4 of the report gives reasons it won't:

- **Reach:** only 61% of families in those schools have a valid mobile number, so up to 39% can't receive a text. Fixing this is not covered by the £2,500 set-up charge as described.
- **Barriers differ:** the lowest-uptake schools have more families who speak another language, and paper forms are often returned incomplete. English-language texts linking to an online portal may not address either problem.
- **Wide variation:** non-reminder uptake ranges from 38% to 79%. Some of those schools may already be at or above 70%, and the weakest may have barriers reminders don't touch.

A realistic projection would give a range, with the effect scaled down for the reach and barrier issues. "Bringing every part of Eastvale up to the level now seen in the west" overstates what the data show. The 70% average also covers reminder schools that aren't all in the west.

"By far the cheapest route" is likewise asserted without a cost-per-additional-vaccinated-child comparison. Mop-up sessions need the same treatment, since they were constrained by staffing rather than shown to be poor value.

## 4. Cost section

The figures check out:

- 4,990 families × 3 × £0.08 ≈ £1,198
- 2,280 families in existing schools × 3 × £0.08 ≈ £547
- Adding the £2,500 set-up gives about £4,250, which is under £5,000.

Two caveats:
- Because of the missing mobile numbers, actual message spend in the 54 schools would be lower, but so would reach. The cost per additional vaccination could be higher than implied.
- Costs for translation, data cleaning, and any extra mop-up staffing aren't included.

## 5. Suggested changes

1. Correct overall uptake to 62.4% and remove or rewrite the "above national ambition" statement.
2. Reword the causal language to "reminder schools had 13 points higher uptake, though the groups differed in important ways", or add the adjusted or baseline-comparison analysis.
3. Remove the "more than any other intervention" claim or support it with data.
4. Present the projected effect in the 54 schools as a range, and address the mobile-number gap and language and form-completion barriers explicitly.
5. Consider recommending a phased or randomised rollout, prioritising the eastern schools, with an evaluation built in. This would give a credible estimate by the end of 2026-27, which the proposed school-level reporting alone won't.
6. Pair reminders with targeted mop-up sessions, translated messages, and data improvement for low-coverage schools, rather than presenting reminders as the whole solution.
